parts.text:
30 Light of wavelength 5.30  10–7
m is incident normally on a diffraction grating. The first-order
maximum is observed at an angle of 15.4 to the direction of the incident light.
What is the angle between the first-order and second-order diffraction maxima?
A
7.7
B
15.4
C
16.7
D
32.1

hints: Notice the first-order maximum at $15.4^{\circ}$ and wavelength $5.30 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$ fix the grating spacing $d$ through $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$.
Use the same $d$ for $n=2$ to get $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin\theta_1$, showing $\theta_2$ is more than twice $\theta_1$ because of the sine.
Calculate $\theta_2$ from $\arcsin(2\sin 15.4^{\circ})$ and then subtract the $15.4^{\circ}$ first-order angle to get the angle between the two maxima.
walkthrough: Write the grating equation for normal incidence: $d\sin\theta = n\lambda$, where $d$ is the slit spacing and $n$ is the order.
For $n=1$, $d\sin 15.4^{\circ} = 5.30 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}$, so $d = \lambda / \sin 15.4^{\circ}$ does not need to be found separately.
For $n=2$ with the same $d$ and $\lambda$: $d\sin\theta_2 = 2\lambda$, so $\sin\theta_2 = 2\sin 15.4^{\circ}$.
Evaluate: $\sin 15.4^{\circ} \approx 0.2656$, so $\sin\theta_2 \approx 0.5312$ and $\theta_2 = \arcsin(0.5312) \approx 32.1^{\circ}$ from the incident direction.
The question asks for the angle between the maxima, so subtract: $32.1^{\circ} - 15.4^{\circ} \approx 16.7^{\circ}$. This is option C.

A.explanation: Halving $15.4^{\circ}$ assumes angle is proportional to order $n$, but $\sin\theta$ is proportional to $n$ so angles spread out with $n$.

B.explanation: Equal spacing of $15.4^{\circ}$ would need $\theta$ proportional to $n$, whereas the grating equation gives $\sin\theta$ proportional to $n$.

C.explanation: Second-order angle is about $32.1^{\circ}$ from the centre, so the separation from $15.4^{\circ}$ is about $16.7^{\circ}$.

D.explanation: About $32.1^{\circ}$ is the second-order angle measured from the incident direction, not the separation between first and second order.
